title: Three Bay Area Hindu Temples Hit in Weeks. All Five Indian-American Lawmakers Just Demanded Answers.
excerpt: In an unprecedented move, every Indian-American member of Congress has written jointly to the DOJ after a wave of pro-Khalistan vandalism struck temples from Hayward to Newark. The State Department and India's foreign minister have also weighed in.
body:
Three Hindu temples in a single stretch of the San Francisco Bay Area have been targeted in quick succession — and for the first time, all five Indian-American members of Congress have united to demand that the Department of Justice explain what it is doing about it.

The latest incident came at Vijay's Sherawali Temple in Hayward, California, where pro-Khalistan graffiti was discovered on the exterior walls. It was the third attack in the area in a matter of weeks: the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Newark had been defaced with anti-India graffiti two weeks earlier, and the Shiv Durga temple in the same area was broken into in between.

## A Pattern, Not an Anomaly

The Bay Area attacks are not isolated. They are the latest in a spreading pattern of vandalism and hate crimes targeting Hindu temples across the United States and Canada. BAPS temples in Sacramento, New York and Southern California's Chino Hills have been hit in recent months, all with anti-Hindu or pro-Khalistan messaging. In Canada, police in Brampton arrested the Sikhs For Justice (SFJ) Canada coordinator in connection with violence at a Hindu temple, and authorities are searching for a suspect who broke into three Hindu temples in a single Canadian city.

The Hindu American Foundation (HAF), which has been tracking the incidents and liaising with temple leaders and local police, has urged all temples to install security cameras and alarm systems.

"Another Bay Area Hindu temple attacked with pro-Khalistan graffiti," HAF said in a statement on X. "The Vijay's Sherawali Temple in Hayward, CA sustained a copycat defacement just two weeks after the Swaminarayan Mandir attack and one week after a theft at the Shiv Durga temple in the same area."

## Congressional Response

The significance of the Congressional letter lies not just in its content but in its signatories. Representatives Raja Krishnamoorthi, Ro Khanna, Shri Thanedar, Pramila Jayapal and Ami Bera — the five Indian-American members of the House — wrote jointly to Kristen Clarke of the DOJ's Civil Rights Division, requesting a formal briefing on the surge in hate crimes targeting Hindus.

It is one of the rare occasions when all five have come together on a single issue, crossing the ideological divides that sometimes separate them.

"Attacks at mandirs from New York to California have contributed to increased collective anxiety among Hindu Americans," they wrote. "Leaders from these impacted communities have expressed there are unfortunately 'no leads' on suspects, leaving many to continue to live in fear and intimidation."

The letter asks the DOJ to explain its strategy for addressing hate crimes against Hindus specifically, and raises pointed questions about whether there is adequate federal oversight and law enforcement coordination.

"The number of incidents and the closeness of the timing of incidents raise troubling questions about linkages and the intent behind them," the lawmakers wrote.

## Diplomatic Dimensions

The attacks have drawn attention at the highest diplomatic levels. The U.S. State Department's Bureau of South and Central Asian Affairs publicly condemned the Newark temple vandalism on X: "We condemn the vandalism of Shri Swaminarayan Mandir Hindu Temple in California. We welcome efforts by the Newark Police Department to ensure that those responsible are held accountable."

India's External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar addressed the issue directly, saying: "As you know, we are concerned about this. Extremists and separatist forces outside India should not get space. Our consulate has lodged a complaint with the government and the police there."

Newark police have termed the Swaminarayan Mandir incident a "targeted act" and assured a thorough investigation.

## A Community on Edge

A 2026 Carnegie Endowment survey of Indian Americans paints a sobering picture of the broader climate. Since the start of 2025, one in four respondents reported being called a slur. Nine per cent said they had been physically threatened, 8 per cent received hate mail, and 4 per cent were victims of physical assault. Half of all respondents reported feeling angry when encountering racist content online, while a third felt anxious or fearful.

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans, many of whom have built their community life around the very temples being targeted, the question is no longer whether this is a pattern. It is whether anyone will stop it before it gets worse.
